title: Reference Method Brief
authority_limit: Consideration authorizes review and revision of a pending proposal. ChatGPT recommendations and cited attachment references are not owner approval, frozen scientific authority, or author-source admission.

items.text:
The brief is trying to turn the FRUIT discussion from “which algorithmic choices look promising?” into a much more concrete question: **what, exactly, would count as a scientifically adequate reference implementation?** There are three substantive proposals in it.

First, for the initial **POINT** case, it proposes that we judge the method in terms of actual astronomical recovery rather than map-level proxies such as RMS or signed moments. In particular, the candidate quantities are **source amplitude/flux, centroid, and source width/shape**. The brief apparently proposes an evaluation-only Gaussian-plus-background fit and provisional tolerances of roughly **5% bias in peak amplitude and width**, with **centroid bias <5% of the source minor-axis width**. Those numbers are not inherited requirements; they are new proposals for us to review.

That distinction matters. The source fit would **not become part of FRUIT**. It is an external ruler with which we ask, “After running this method, did we get the source back?” That is much closer to the scientific question we actually care about. For a POINT observation, I think this is the right conceptual direction, although I would want to scrutinize whether **peak amplitude** is really the primary flux estimator. Peak amplitude is entangled with recovered beam width; integrated flux or an appropriately normalized PSF amplitude may be a cleaner primary photometric quantity.

Second, the brief proposes a way out of the weighting rabbit hole: **use uniform weighting as a reference definition without claiming that it is scientifically optimal**. That's an important nuance. The weighting exercise showed that detector weighting matters: the N4U-like weighting reduced measured background RMS substantially in the real examples, but it also changed recovered source-template amplitudes by 12–32%, and we didn't have enough evidence to decide whether those changes were improvements or biases. So neither weighting scheme won.

The proposed solution is therefore something like:

> For purposes of defining a reproducible reference method, use uniform weighting because it is simple and completely specified. Do **not** interpret that choice as a recommendation for production Citlali, optimal sensitivity, or correct inverse-variance weighting.

I think that's defensible **if our immediate objective is a reference implementation rather than a production prescription**. Uniform weighting then becomes part of the experimental control. Its known shortcomings are actually acceptable because we're not pretending otherwise. We'd be saying, in effect, “Here is the simplest fully defined FRUIT method against which later improvements can be measured.”

Third, the brief says we still need an **exact reference record**. This is more than documenting “ordinary mapmaking + FRUIT.” We need to bind every choice required to reproduce the calculation. The existing frozen work already gives us much of the architecture—residual formation, relearning of PTC on the sky-subtracted timestream, recurrence roles, etc.—so we're not reopening those decisions. What's left is the numerical plumbing where the contracts intentionally remained open: the exact coefficient/weighting rule and MAP handoff (Q02-C and successors), effective PTC grouping/rank/support choices (Q03), MAP support/edge behavior (Q04), whatever response/inference information is actually necessary for the recovery claim (parts of Q01/Q05), and the exact continuation/stopping/terminal-selection/failure behavior (Q06).

There is also a subtle issue with the **historical control**. The historical Citlali behavior is supposed to remain our mandatory comparison, but the brief found that we don't yet have a completely authoritative record of the *exact executed historical configuration*. We have source/configuration evidence and historical settings, but apparently not enough to claim that every numerical setting is bound to the actual execution. The brief correctly refuses to silently fill those holes from templates or from our recent single-pass reductions.

So I see the proposed progression as:

**freeze the scientific question → define a deliberately simple reference method → establish source-recovery requirements → run only the minimum experiment necessary to determine whether that reference satisfies them.**

That is quite different from what we were doing in the weighting investigation. We would no longer ask, “Is N4U better than uniform?” We'd ask something like, **“For a POINT source of known truth, does this completely specified FRUIT reference recover its photometry, position, and PSF within our declared tolerances?”** If not, the failure tells us specifically which piece of the reference method needs reconsideration.

The parts I think deserve *our* attention before approving the brief are therefore not all of Q01–Q06. They are much narrower: **(1)** what is the primary photometric recovery quantity—peak, PSF amplitude, integrated flux, or more than one; **(2)** whether 5% is the scientifically justified tolerance and whether the centroid tolerance should be expressed relative to beam size or in arcseconds; and **(3)** whether we're comfortable declaring uniform weighting the intentionally non-optimal reference rather than leaving weighting formally unresolved.

Of those, **#1 is the one I'd tackle first**. Once we say precisely what “recover the POINT source” means, the tolerances and the evidence we need become much easier to reason about.

Reassess this.  It seems like in doing this we are heading down the aforementioned (and desired) road of splitting FRUIT by its program intents.  POINT has different requirements and priors from OOF, etc.  Is this testing the time to make that split, or should we just take POINT for now and see where that takes us?

**I would make the intent distinction explicit now, but develop and test POINT first.** Those are compatible choices. The important qualification is that we should **split the scientific requirements and feedback policies—not prematurely create separate FRUIT implementations or launch parallel development campaigns.**

My previous answer was too loose about calling the proposed method *the reference method*. It should be **a POINT reference method within the shared, mode-aware FRUIT framework**. Otherwise, choices made to recover a localized pointing source could quietly become requirements that OOF and extended-emission science later have to work around.

This is also consistent with your September 9 directive: observing-mode policies belong in the contract from the outset, while their numerical recipes develop experimentally. We are not discovering a new architectural requirement here; we need to carry the existing one into this brief. fileciteturn2file0L122-L140

## What should split now—and what should not

I would distinguish three levels:

| Level | What we should do now |
|---|---|
| **Shared FRUIT machinery** | Retain the existing recurrence, data/model relationships, producer boundaries, and runtime Learn–Consider–Apply responsibilities. |
| **Intent-dependent feedback policy** | Explicitly identify which priors, evidence, admission rules, and numerical model-construction choices belong to the observing intent. Fully specify only the first POINT candidate. |
| **Scientific acceptance criteria** | Make the initial recovery requirements explicitly POINT-specific. Do not extend POINT results to OOF, BEAM, or SCIENCE without their own evidence. |

The shared machinery already has the essential scientific structure: start from the immutable measured-data parent, subtract the current feedback model, relearn PTC on that sky-subtracted input, reconstruct the total, and re-infer a replacement feedback model that can admit **and revoke** content. None of that becomes a different principle simply because the observation is OOF rather than POINT. fileciteturn2file0L34-L83

The principal intent-dependent step is **how we interpret the reconstructed total and construct the next astronomical feedback model**. That is where “we expect a dominant localized source” and “we expect a potentially faint, highly distorted out-of-focus response” lead to different permissible assumptions. This policy must exist within FRUIT’s runtime learning, consideration, and application—not merely in an external scoring script. fileciteturn2file0L95-L118 fileciteturn2file0L274-L282

But recognizing that distinction does **not** establish that each intent requires a wholly different algorithm. Experiments might show that several intents share one inference family with different parameters; others may need genuinely different policies. **We know the objectives and allowed priors differ. We have not yet established how much the numerical methods must differ.**

## Why “just take POINT and see where it leads” needs a boundary

Taking POINT first is sensible. Treating POINT as an unspecified stand-in for all FRUIT is not.

Consider a candidate policy that identifies a bright central feature and admits nearby emission around it. Even excellent POINT recovery would not establish that this policy is appropriate for OOF, because the OOF requirements explicitly allow no useful central anchor, faint distributed structure, and complicated morphology. A bright-core requirement would exclude part of the intended OOF domain before the iteration even had a chance to recover it. fileciteturn2file0L126-L140

There is a subtler danger even within POINT. A tight position prior could make the result look well behaved while suppressing the pointing offset we need to measure. A tight width prior could suppress evidence of defocus. Your directive already rules out both shortcuts. fileciteturn2file0L126-L130

That matters especially in an iterative feedback method: the model influences the next residual, hence the next learned cleaning state, and is subsequently rejoined. Agreement with the assumed model is therefore not automatically independent evidence that the data support it. Your directive’s fixed-cleaner example illustrates how an erroneous model component can survive through the model path even when the iteration appears stable. fileciteturn2file0L238-L246

So the guardrail should be:

> **POINT is our first development case, not our definition of what astronomical signal must look like.**

That permits focused progress without allowing convenient POINT assumptions to become hidden universal constraints.

## I would also revise the emphasis of the POINT test

My previous response put too much emphasis on deciding between peak amplitude and integrated flux as the first scientific question. That is important, but it should follow the observing purpose.

For this POINT reference, I would organize the requirements around **recovering the pointing offset while preserving the source-response information needed to assess width, distortion, and photometry**. The earlier directive specifically calls for judging pointing recovery without nominal-position bias. fileciteturn2file0L264-L268

That changes how we should view the proposed Gaussian-plus-background evaluation fit. It can be a useful measurement tool for an appropriate subset of POINT responses, but it should not silently define the entire POINT domain. If the response is distorted, disagreement with a Gaussian could be a limitation of the evaluator rather than a failure of FRUIT.

It also reinforces the separation we discussed earlier:

**Using a Gaussian to measure an output is not the same decision as feeding a Gaussian model back into the iteration.** The latter changes the numerical sky-estimation policy and needs its own explicit justification. The existing directive already separates admission, retained-flux estimation, and subsequent transformations, including fitted-source replacement. fileciteturn2file0L103-L120

Likewise, the proposed 5% tolerances should remain proposed requirements for a declared POINT domain—not generic FRUIT accuracy requirements.

## How much cross-mode work is necessary before POINT testing?

**A small design check, not a second experimental campaign.**

Before proceeding, I would use OOF as a counterexample against the proposed shared machinery: could we replace the POINT policy with one that admits distributed, non-Gaussian structure without a bright core, while leaving the recurrence intact? Are localization and shape assumptions attached to the policy rather than embedded in the engine? Could the evaluator change without changing the feedback rule?

That is enough to expose the most obvious POINT-specific assumptions. It does not require designing the OOF estimator, selecting its thresholds, processing its archive, or solving its recovery metrics now.

Similarly, we should not force a premature one-to-one correspondence between an observing-program label and an algorithm. Your SCIENCE requirements already recognize mixed fields and different bright/faint regimes; even OOF may eventually distinguish near-focus from strongly defocused cases. Named intents should make assumptions explicit, not become rigid categories that obscure them. fileciteturn2file0L138-L140 fileciteturn2file0L152-L164

## What I would change in the brief

I would make three bounded changes:

1. **Name the scope explicitly:** “Initial POINT reference within mode-aware FRUIT.” State what POINT conditions it addresses and what its results will not establish.
2. **Separate shared decisions from POINT choices:** reuse the frozen recurrence and existing interfaces; place the proposed priors, feedback recipe, evaluator, and recovery targets in the POINT-specific portion. Identify only concrete interface omissions.
3. **Keep the numerical work POINT-only:** complete the exact first reference recipe and its focused test. Leave OOF and the other policies undeveloped rather than filling them with POINT defaults.

Any adopted weighting rule would likewise be a setting of that exact reference, not a universal FRUIT requirement. This does not reopen the weighting exploration or turn uniform weighting into an approved policy by implication.

The resulting experiment would answer two different questions: **does the shared machinery execute the intended recurrence correctly, and does this particular POINT policy recover the relevant information over its declared test domain?** It would not answer whether the same policy is adequate for OOF.

**My recommendation is therefore: make the policy boundary explicit now, then take POINT first.** Do not wait for POINT development to determine the architecture accidentally, and do not require all observing intents to be numerically specified before making progress on one.
